subject: economics
topicDisplay: International Trade and the Global Economy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In international trade, what is meant by an 'import'?
options: A good or service bought from another country
A good or service sold to another country
A tax placed on foreign goods
A limit on the quantity of goods traded
questions.explain: Imports are goods and services that a country buys in from abroad.

questions.q: What is meant by an 'export'?
options: A good or service sold to another country
A good or service bought from another country
A subsidy given to domestic producers
A quota on incoming goods
questions.explain: Exports are goods and services produced domestically and sold to buyers abroad.

questions.q: Which of the following is a benefit to a country of taking part in international trade?
options: Access to a wider variety of goods and services
A guaranteed government budget surplus
The removal of all domestic competition
A permanently fixed exchange rate
questions.explain: Trade lets consumers buy goods that cannot be produced domestically or are cheaper abroad, widening choice.

questions.q: How does specialisation encourage countries to trade with one another?
options: Countries produce what they are relatively best at and exchange for the rest
Countries produce every good themselves to avoid trade
Countries raise tariffs to protect all industries
Countries stop producing goods altogether
questions.explain: By specialising in goods they produce most efficiently and trading, countries can consume more overall.

questions.q: What is a tariff?
options: A tax placed on imported goods
A limit on the number of imports allowed
A payment made to domestic producers
A ban on trading with a country
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price and can protect domestic industry.

questions.q: What is the most likely effect of a government placing a tariff on imported cars?
options: Imported cars become more expensive for domestic buyers
Imported cars become cheaper for domestic buyers
Domestic car producers face more foreign competition
The country's exports automatically increase
questions.explain: A tariff adds a tax to the import price, making foreign cars dearer and protecting domestic producers.

questions.q: What does the balance of payments record?
options: Financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world
The total value of goods sold within a country
The government's spending and taxation each year
The number of people employed in an economy
questions.explain: The balance of payments is a record of all economic transactions between one country and others.

questions.q: A trade deficit occurs when a country's:
options: Imports are greater than its exports
Exports are greater than its imports
Government spending is greater than tax revenue
Exchange rate is fixed
questions.explain: A trade deficit means the value of imports exceeds the value of exports.

questions.q: A trade surplus occurs when a country's:
options: Exports are greater than its imports
Imports are greater than its exports
Currency appreciates in value
Tariffs are removed
questions.explain: A trade surplus means the value of exports exceeds the value of imports.

questions.q: The balance of trade in goods is calculated as:
options: The value of exports of goods minus the value of imports of goods
The value of imports of goods minus the value of exports of goods
The value of exports of goods plus the value of imports of goods
Total government revenue minus total spending
questions.explain: The balance of trade is exports minus imports; a positive figure is a surplus and a negative figure a deficit.

questions.q: In one year a country exports £400bn of goods and imports £550bn of goods. What is its balance of trade in goods?
options: A deficit of £150bn
A surplus of £150bn
A deficit of £950bn
A surplus of £400bn
questions.explain: Exports (£400bn) minus imports (£550bn) gives -£150bn, a trade deficit.

questions.q: A country records exports of services worth £300bn and imports of services worth £220bn. Its balance of trade in services is:
options: A surplus of £80bn
A deficit of £80bn
A surplus of £520bn
A deficit of £220bn
questions.explain: Exports (£300bn) exceed imports (£220bn) by £80bn, giving a services trade surplus.

questions.q: What is an exchange rate?
options: The price of one currency in terms of another
The tax charged on imported goods
The total value of a country's exports
The rate of inflation in an economy
questions.explain: An exchange rate shows how much of one currency is needed to buy another.

questions.q: When a currency rises in value against other currencies, this is known as:
options: An appreciation
A depreciation
A devaluation
A deficit
questions.explain: An appreciation is a rise in the value of a currency in a floating exchange rate system.

questions.q: According to the mnemonic SPICED, when the pound is strong:
options: Imports are cheaper and exports are dearer
Imports are dearer and exports are cheaper
Both imports and exports are cheaper
Both imports and exports are dearer
questions.explain: SPICED stands for Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.

questions.q: If the pound depreciates against the US dollar, the likely effect on UK exports to the USA is that they become:
options: Cheaper for American buyers, so exports tend to rise
More expensive for American buyers, so exports tend to fall
Unchanged in price for American buyers
Banned from sale in the USA
questions.explain: A weaker pound lowers the dollar price of UK goods, making exports more competitive abroad.

questions.q: The exchange rate is £1 = $2. A television made in the USA is priced at $400. What is its price in pounds?
questions.explain: At £1 = $2, dividing the $400 price by 2 gives a UK price of £200.

questions.q: The pound appreciates from £1 = €1.10 to £1 = €1.20. A UK exporter selling a product for £100 will find that in euros the product now costs a European buyer:
options: More than before, at €120 instead of €110
Less than before, at €100 instead of €110
Exactly the same at €110
Nothing, as the euro price is unaffected
questions.explain: A stronger pound means each £100 converts to more euros (€120), making UK exports dearer abroad.

questions.q: Which statement best describes globalisation?
options: The increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies
The removal of a single country from international trade
A tax charged on all imported goods
The fixing of exchange rates by governments
questions.explain: Globalisation is the growing interconnection of economies through trade, investment and the movement of goods, capital and labour.

questions.q: Which of the following has most contributed to the growth of globalisation?
options: Improvements in transport and communications technology
The introduction of higher tariffs worldwide
A fall in the number of multinational companies
A reduction in international investment
questions.explain: Cheaper transport and faster communication have made it easier for firms to trade and operate across borders.

questions.q: A multinational company (MNC) is a business that:
options: Operates and produces in more than one country
Only sells goods within its home country
Is owned entirely by the government
Trades only with neighbouring countries
questions.explain: Multinationals have operations, production or offices located in more than one country.

questions.q: Which of the following is a possible drawback of globalisation for a developed economy?
options: Domestic jobs may be lost as production moves to lower-cost countries
Consumers lose access to a variety of foreign goods
Trade between countries decreases sharply
Multinational companies stop investing abroad
questions.explain: Firms may relocate production to cheaper locations abroad, causing job losses in higher-cost economies.
